practice.q: Define personality as given in the chapter.
practice.answer: Personality is the unique, relatively enduring set of internal and external aspects of a person's character that influence behaviour in different situations. The chapter's working version describes it as an enduring and unique cluster of characteristics that may change in response to different situations, while noting that each theorist offers his or her own definition.

Historical determinism is the view that personality is basically fixed in the early years of life, by about age 5, and changes little afterwards. Adult personality is seen as an elaboration of themes laid down in childhood. It is one position on the issue of whether we are dependent on or independent of childhood.

Reliability is the consistency of response to an assessment device: a reliable test gives similar scores when taken again. Validity is the extent to which a device measures what it is intended to measure. An unreliable or invalid test cannot be trusted to assess personality or predict behaviour.

practice.q: Explain the different ways of looking at personality.
practice.answer:
The chapter offers several everyday ways of understanding personality. First, Adams (1954) suggested that personality is captured by what we mean when we say "I", which sums up our likes, dislikes, fears, virtues, strengths and weaknesses.

Second, the word comes from the Latin persona, an actor's mask, dating back to about 1500. This suggests personality is our public face, the impression we make on others. However, the authors argue personality also includes inner social and emotional qualities that may be hidden.

Third, personality refers to stable and predictable characteristics. It is not rigid, since a calm person can become panicky, but it resists sudden change. The 1960s person-situation debate (Mischel) ended, as Funder (2001) noted, with the interactionist view that traits, situations and their interaction all matter.

Fourth, personality implies uniqueness. We notice similarities among people, yet each person has special qualities distinguishing him or her from everyone else, which is why two people in the same situation can react quite differently.

Combining these, personality is an enduring and unique cluster of characteristics that may change in different situations, though each theorist defines it in his or her own way. Understanding these competing versions, the many ways of defining the word "I", is the purpose of studying personality theories.

practice.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of self-report inventories, with reference to the MMPI.
practice.answer:
Self-report inventories ask people to answer questions about their own behaviour and feelings in various situations. The best known is the MMPI, the world's most widely used test, translated into over 140 languages. It has 567 true-false items covering health, attitudes, family and work, and neurotic and psychotic tendencies, with clinical scales such as depression, paranoia and schizophrenia.

Advantages: self-reports are the most objective approach, scored quickly by automated programmes giving a full diagnostic profile. The MMPI has items to detect faking and carelessness; it distinguishes genuine from faked pain and PTSD and separates neurotics from psychotics. Self-reports can also be taken online, which is cheaper, faster, more objective and prevents looking ahead, with results matching paper versions.

Disadvantages: the MMPI is long, and some people lose motivation; personal items may seem an invasion of privacy, especially in job testing. Self-reports may not suit people of below-normal intelligence or poor reading skills. Small wording changes alter results (Schwarz, 1999), and people tend to give socially desirable answers and can fake easily (Holtgraves, 2004; McDaniel et al., 2009). Even the mentally ill can learn online to hide symptoms on the MMPI.

Overall, despite these limits, the MMPI remains a valuable diagnostic and research tool.

practice.q: Explain how social media and personality influence each other.
practice.answer:
The chapter raises three questions about personality and social media.

Real self online: US and German studies found online profiles convey personality at least as accurately as face-to-face contact (Gosling et al., 2007; Back et al., 2010). But many people present themselves as more emotionally stable than they are (Blumer & Doring, 2012), and introverted, lonely, socially awkward people express their true selves more easily online (Marriott & Buchanan, 2014). Inappropriate posts create false impressions that can affect jobs (Goodman et al., 2014).

Social media shaping personality: excessive internet use in Chinese adolescents was linked to anxiety and depression (Lam & Peng, 2010); heavy use lowers well-being and relationship quality; students who contacted parents via social networking felt more lonely and anxious than those who phoned (Gentzler et al., 2011). Excessive users are lonelier and lower in self-esteem, and overuse may become addictive and alter brain areas linked to depression (Mosher, 2011).

Personality shaping use: extraverted and narcissistic people use Facebook more and narcissistic teens update status more. Heavy users are more extraverted and open but less conscientious and emotionally stable. In Australia, extraverts made more calls, while neurotic, shy people texted more. Trolls are mostly male, about 29, and high in sadism.

Thus social media both shapes and reflects personality.

practice.q: Discuss the role of culture in shaping personality.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Psychology widely accepts that culture shapes personality. Cross-cultural psychology has shown that personality is formed by both genetic and environmental influences, and Triandis and Suh (2002) argued that cultural influences are among the most important environmental ones. The chapter supports this with immigrant studies, neuroscience and research on beliefs, individualism, child-rearing and self-enhancement.

Evidence of cultural change and difference

Japanese who emigrated to the US became more American in personality than those who stayed (Gungor et al., 2013). Chinese immigrants who had lived in Canada for 10 years or more scored higher in extraversion than recent immigrants or Hong Kong Chinese (McCrae et al., 1998). Asian-American students reported more negative emotions in social situations than European Americans (Lee et al., 2006), while Westerners are more optimistic and rate their teams, cities and friends as superior (Endo et al., 2000). Cultural neuroscience has even found Eastern and Western differences in brain responses to the same stimuli, matching levels of dominance or submissiveness (Freeman et al., 2009).

Beliefs about destiny

The concept of karma in India and other Hindu or Buddhist countries is a fatalistic view in which present and past actions decide future fate. It may encourage a passive, accepting personality, unlike the American stress on free choice and effort. East-West differences in fate attribution are large, but weaken as cultures such as China modernise (Wong, Shaw, & Ng, 2010).

Individualism and collectivism

Individualistic societies emphasise personal freedom and choice; collectivist ones stress group norms and roles. Australians valued individuality more than Japanese (Kashima et al., 2004). Individualistic cultures show more extraversion, self-esteem, optimism and well-being; a study of 400 million people in 63 countries tied individualism to well-being (Fischer & Boer, 2011). US students scored higher in self-efficacy than Japanese students, and European Americans pursued goals for personal satisfaction while Asian Americans pursued goals that please important others (Oishi & Diener, 2001). A recently arrived Asian job applicant may score low on assertiveness and be unfairly judged deficient.

Child-rearing practices

American parenting tends to be democratic and permissive, while Asian and Arab parenting is more authoritarian. Arab adolescents accepted authoritarian parenting, felt close to parents and showed no harm to mental health (Dwairy et al., 2006). More assimilated Turkish mothers in Germany stressed individualistic goals (Durgel et al., 2009).

Self-enhancement and self-effacement

Self-enhancement, aggressive self-promotion, is higher among Canadians, Americans and Israelis; self-effacement is higher among Japanese and Chinese (Heine et al., 2000; Church et al., 2014). Nordic Janteloven promotes humility, and Americans self-enhanced more than Norwegians (Silvera & Seger, 2004). Even Spain and the Netherlands differ in family versus individualistic values.

Conclusion

Culture influences traits, emotions, self-views, motivation and even brain activity. However, research is still concentrated in English-speaking countries and on American college students, with little from Africa and South America. Personality theories and tests must therefore be applied with cultural sensitivity rather than assumed to be universal.

practice.q: Describe the major methods of personality assessment and evaluate their strengths and limitations.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Assessment means measuring or evaluating personality. It is used by clinical psychologists for diagnosis and therapy, school psychologists for adjustment problems, industrial/organisational psychologists for selection, counselling psychologists for career matching, and researchers. Good techniques must be reliable (consistent) and valid (measuring what they claim). The chapter describes five approaches.

1. Self-report inventories

People answer questions about their own behaviour and feelings. The MMPI, the most widely used test, has 567 true-false items and scales such as depression and paranoia, plus faking checks. Strengths: most objective, quick automated scoring, can be given online with results equal to paper, and people disclose more online. Limitations: length, privacy concerns, unsuitable for low reading ability, sensitivity to wording (Schwarz, 1999) and social desirability or faking.

2. Projective techniques

Inspired by Freud, they assume people project needs and fears onto ambiguous stimuli. The Rorschach (1921) uses 10 inkblots scored for movement, figures and whole or partial responses; Exner's Comprehensive System tries to standardise it. The TAT (Morgan & Murray, 1935) uses 19 pictures and a blank card for storytelling and is useful for researching needs for achievement, affiliation and power. Word association and sentence completion are other forms. Strengths: they aim to probe the unconscious and remain widely used. Limitations: subjective interpretation, low reliability, validity and inter-scorer reliability; validity research favours the MMPI.

3. Clinical interviews

The psychologist explores past and present life, relationships and problems, observing appearance, expressions, insight and contact with reality, often guided by MMPI results. Strength: rich information. Limitation: interpretation is subjective and affected by the interviewer's orientation, so interviews work best alongside objective tools.

4. Behavioural assessment

An observer evaluates behaviour in a situation; observers who know the person well are more accurate (Connelly & Ones, 2010). Buss and Plomin's EASI survey had mothers rate twins' temperaments. Strength: it records actual behaviour rather than what people say about themselves. Limitation: it depends on the observer's familiarity and skill. Informal observation in counselling, such as noting facial expressions, nervous gestures and appearance, is less systematic than formal procedures but still gives valuable insights for diagnosis.

5. Thought and experience sampling

People record their own thoughts over time; experience sampling adds context, often prompted by beepers or smartphones. A 28-day diary study showed academic issues as students' main stressor (Park et al., 2004). Limitations: participants forget, data may come only from conscientious people, and moods colour reports; still, data are comparable to self-reports.

Conclusion

No single method is perfect, and the theorists themselves used whichever methods suited their theories, ranging from dream interpretation to computer-scored tests. Objective self-reports are most reliable but open to faking; projective and interview methods give depth but are subjective. Results can also be affected by gender, ethnicity and culture, so assessors should combine methods and interpret scores with cultural sensitivity.

practice.q: Compare the clinical, experimental, virtual and correlational methods of personality research.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Personality researchers choose methods based on whether they study overt behaviour, conscious experience or unconscious forces. The four major methods are clinical, experimental, virtual and correlational. All depend on objective observation, and good research also needs controlled, systematic conditions and duplication and verifiability.

Clinical method

The main tool is the case study, a detailed history of an individual drawn from many sources. Freud traced Katharina's anxiety attacks to early sexual experiences and Lucy's hallucinations to rejected love, then generalised to everyone. Other clinical tools include tests, interviews and dream analysis. Strength: it offers a window into the depths of personality and is central to psychoanalytic theory. Weaknesses: data are subjective, open to the therapist's bias, rely on childhood memories that may be distorted and unverifiable, and lack precision and control.

Experimental method

An experiment determines the effect of a variable on behaviour by allowing only that variable to operate. The independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is the measured behaviour. Randomly selected experimental and control groups are compared before and after. Bandura measured children's aggression, exposed one group to an aggressive adult and a control group to non-aggressive adults, and found only the first group became aggressive, showing that aggression is learned by imitation. Strength: the most precise method, able to establish cause and effect. Weaknesses: ethical and safety limits (children cannot be removed from parents to test child-rearing), and subjects who know they are observed may change behaviour or try to please or frustrate the experimenter.

Virtual research

Online tests, surveys and experiments, often using Amazon's Mechanical Turk, are faster and cheaper and reach more diverse samples than college campuses. Weaknesses: web users are younger, richer and more educated; older, poor, visually impaired and non-English speakers are under-represented; non-responders differ in personality; response rates are about 10 percent lower; honesty is hard to verify. Still, online and laboratory results are generally similar.

Correlational method

Researchers measure the relationship between existing variables rather than manipulating them, without experimental and control groups. For example, students high in need for achievement earned higher grades (Atkinson et al., 1976). The correlation coefficient, from +1.00 to -1.00, shows direction and strength. It is used to establish test reliability and validity and for practical prediction, such as college entrance tests. Weakness: it cannot show cause and effect; a shyness-self-esteem link might run either way or be caused by a third variable.

Conclusion

The experimental method gives the most control and causal certainty, the correlational method is excellent for prediction, virtual research adds speed and diversity, and the clinical method gives depth at the cost of objectivity. Researchers choose according to the aspect of personality being studied, since a method suited to one aspect may be inappropriate for another, and in practice they often combine methods to offset each one's weaknesses.
